knowledgePoints.name: What an agent is
knowledgePoints.teach:
An agent is not a model. It is an autonomous version of Claude running both sides of the messaging loop with no human in the middle: it receives a task, picks a tool, and keeps going until it decides the task is done.

The word that does the work there is both. In a chat application a person supplies every user turn. In an agent, your code supplies them — and what it supplies is tool results.

You own the loop and the tools. Claude owns the reasoning.

Nothing about the API changes. It is the same stateless messages.create, called repeatedly, with the array growing each time.

questions.q: What distinguishes an agent from an ordinary chat integration?
options: It relies on a more capable model tier
Claude runs both sides; tool results are turns
It maintains conversation state server-side
It streams rather than returning one response
questions.explain: The human turn is replaced by a tool result your code produces. That is the whole structural difference.

questions.q: In an agent, who owns what?
options: You own the loop and tools; Claude reasons
Claude owns the loop; you own the reasoning
Anthropic owns the loop; you own the tools
You own the tools; Claude owns loop and reasoning
questions.explain: Loop and tools yours, reasoning Claude's — and that split is exactly what managed agents later renegotiate.

knowledgePoints.name: The five steps
knowledgePoints.teach:
1. Send a message to Claude with tools available.
  2. Claude responds with either a final answer or a tool-use request.
  3. Your code executes that tool.
  4. You send the result back as a tool_result block.
  5. Repeat until stop_reason is end_turn.
while True:
    resp = client.messages.create(model=M, max_tokens=1024,
                                  messages=messages, tools=tools)
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break                                   # ← step 5
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content})
    results = [run(b) for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})

The loop's continue condition is stop_reason == tool_use. Its exit condition is end_turn.

Everything else in this cluster is a refinement of these five lines.

questions.q: What ends an agent loop?
options: The tools array has been exhausted
A maximum iteration count is reached
The response contains a text block
stop_reason comes back as end_turn
questions.explain: end_turn. An iteration cap is a sensible safety net you add, but it is not what the loop is defined by.

questions.q: In which step does your own code do the work?
options: Step 2, where Claude decides which tool
Step 3, where the requested tool is run
Step 5, where the loop condition is checked
Step 1, where the tools are all defined
questions.explain: Claude asks; you execute. Step 3 is where your function actually runs.

options: Send with tools → tool_use → execute → tool_result → repeat
Send with tools → execute → tool_use → end_turn → repeat
Execute → send with tools → tool_result → tool_use → end
Send with tools → end_turn → execute → tool_result → loop
reviewQuestions.explain: Claude requests before you execute, and end_turn is the exit rather than a stage.

reviewQuestions.q: Does the agent loop require a different API endpoint?
options: Yes — /agents instead of /messages
Yes, once more than one tool is defined
No — messages.create in a loop, array growing
No, but it needs the streaming endpoint
reviewQuestions.explain: Same stateless call, called in a loop. The agency is in your code, not in a different endpoint.

knowledgePoints.name: Name, description, input_schema
knowledgePoints.teach:
A tool is a JSON object with three parts:

{
  "name":        "get_weather",
  "description": "Get the current weather for a city. Use when the user asks
                  about conditions, temperature, or whether to bring a coat.
                  Returns temperature in Celsius and a one-word condition.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}},
    "required": ["city"]
  }
}

input_schema is standard JSON Schema — a general data-validation specification that long predates any of this and is not AI-specific. If you have written an OpenAPI spec, you already know it.

Convention: name a schema function_name_schema so it pairs visibly with the function it describes. And you can hand your function's source to Claude and ask it to generate the schema.

questions.q: What are the three parts of a tool definition?
options: name, handler, output_schema
name, description, input_schema
name, input_schema, output_schema
description, input_schema, tool_choice
questions.explain: Name, description, input_schema. There is no output schema — what a tool returns is described in prose, in the description.

questions.q: What kind of specification is input_schema?
options: Standard JSON Schema, a general spec
An Anthropic format for tool arguments
A TypeScript type definition, compiled
OpenAPI, restricted to request bodies
questions.explain: Plain JSON Schema. Nothing about it is AI-specific.

reviewQuestions.q: Which field describes what a tool returns?
options: output_schema on the definition
The input_schema's `returns` property
The description, in prose; there is none
Nothing; Claude infers it from results
reviewQuestions.explain: The description carries it. That is one reason the guidance is three or four sentences rather than one.

knowledgePoints.name: The field Claude actually reads
knowledgePoints.teach:
The description is what Claude reads to decide whether and when to call the tool.

Not the name. Not the schema. The description. Which makes it the single highest-leverage string in an agent, and:

Vague descriptions are the number one cause of agents misfiring or not using available tools.

The symptom is distinctive: nothing errors. The tool works perfectly when called. It just never gets called, or gets called for the wrong requests, and the agent produces a confident answer it invented instead.

Aim for three or four sentences covering:

  • what it does,
  • when to use it — the part most people omit,
  • what it returns.
WeakStrong
“Searches the database.”“Search customer orders by email address. Use when the user asks about a past order, a delivery date, or a refund status. Returns up to 10 orders, newest first, each with an order id, status, and total.”

questions.q: An agent has a working search tool and never calls it. Where do you look first?
options: The input_schema, for a field it cannot fill
The model tier, perhaps too small for tools
The temperature, suppressing the tool calls
The description, which drives the selection
questions.explain: Selection is a description problem. It is named as the number one cause of agents ignoring tools they have.

questions.q: Which three things should a tool description cover?
options: What it does, when to use it, what it returns
What it does, who owns it, how long it takes
Its name, its arguments, and its error codes
What it does, what it costs, when it changed
questions.explain: Three or four sentences on those three points. 'When to use it' is the one most often missing.

reviewQuestions.q: Why is a tool that is never called a hard bug to notice?
options: The API returns a warning that is easy to miss
It only ever manifests under production load
The tool_use block comes back and is discarded
Nothing errors — it just answers without it
reviewQuestions.explain: There is no failure signal. The agent produces a plausible invented answer instead of a grounded one.

reviewQuestions.q: Two tools have overlapping purposes and Claude keeps picking the wrong one. What do you fix?
options: Rename them so that they sort differently
Remove one and merge their two schemas together
Sharpen both, especially 'when to use it'
Set tool_choice to any on every request
reviewQuestions.explain: Selection between tools is decided by description. Making each one's applicability explicit is the fix.

knowledgePoints.name: Four invariants
knowledgePoints.teach:
The reliable sequence, stated precisely:

  1. Send the user's request and the tool definitions.
  2. Receive an assistant response containing text and/or tool_use blocks.
  3. Execute each requested tool.
  4. Send the complete assistant content back, then a user message containing matching tool_result blocks.
  5. Request the final answer.

Four things must hold, and each has a characteristic failure:

InvariantBreak it and…
Preserve the complete assistant content array, not just the visible textthe tool_use block vanishes and the tool_result has nothing to answer
Each tool_result references its matching tool_use idthe request is rejected as malformed
Every tool_use in a turn gets a resultthe request is rejected — no partial answers
The original tool schemas stay on the follow-up requestClaude no longer knows what the tools were

questions.q: You append only the assistant's text to the history and send a tool_result. What breaks?
options: The tool_use is gone; the result answers nothing
Nothing — the visible text is what matters
The tool schemas are lost from the tools array
stop_reason turns into end_turn prematurely
questions.explain: Preserve the complete content array. The tool_use block is part of the conversation, not presentation.

questions.q: Claude requests three tools in one turn and you return two results. What happens?
options: The request is rejected; each id needs one
Claude proceeds with the two it was given
The third one gets retried automatically
The third is treated as an error result
questions.explain: All or nothing. Each tool_use id must be answered.

knowledgePoints.name: Tool input is untrusted input
knowledgePoints.teach:
The arguments in a tool_use block were produced by a model, from text that may have come from a user. They are not from your code, and they are not vetted.

Treat tool inputs as untrusted data. Validate authorisation, arguments, timeouts, and side effects before execution.

def run_refund(args, ctx):
    order = db.get(args["order_id"])
    if order.customer_id != ctx.customer_id:   # authorisation — not the model's job
        return error("not your order")
    if args["amount_cents"] > order.total_cents:
        return error("amount exceeds order total")
    ...

The schema already checked that order_id is a string and amount_cents is an integer. It has no opinion about whether this user may refund that order — and neither does the model. Authorisation lives in your executor or it lives nowhere.

The prompt-injection case makes this concrete: a document Claude reads can contain instructions, and if reading it can cause a refund, the document can cause a refund.

questions.q: Where does authorisation for a tool call belong?
options: In the description, as an instruction to follow
In your executor, before the side effect runs
In the input_schema, as one required field
In the system prompt, as a standing site rule
questions.explain: Only code can enforce. A prompt-level rule is a request, and untrusted content in context can compete with it.

questions.q: The schema validated the tool input. What has that established?
options: That the arguments are safe to act on now
That the user authorised this exact action
That the values exist in your own database
That the shape and types are right — no more
questions.explain: Shape, not permission. Same boundary as structured output: schemas check structure, code checks truth.

reviewQuestions.q: Which must accompany the follow-up request after a tool runs?
options: Only the tool_result blocks themselves
The original tool schemas, still in tools
A fresh system prompt describing results
The tool's source code, for reference
reviewQuestions.explain: The schemas stay. Each call is stateless, so dropping them leaves Claude without the definitions it is reasoning about.

knowledgePoints.name: Two changes, no more
knowledgePoints.teach:
Claude reads all the descriptions you provide and picks per turn — sometimes several tools at once, sometimes one after another across turns.

Adding a tool is two edits:

tools.append(get_weather_schema)         # 1. declare it

def dispatch(block):                      # 2. add a case
    if   block.name == "get_weather": return get_weather(**block.input)
    elif block.name == "search_orders": return search_orders(**block.input)
    ...

Declare it, dispatch it. Nothing about the loop changes.

That is the payoff of the loop being generic: it does not know or care how many tools exist. Which also means the thing that scales badly is not your code — it is the quality of your descriptions, since every added tool makes selection harder.

questions.q: What has to change to go from one tool to five?
options: The loop, to take multiple tool_use blocks
The model tier, for the bigger schema set
The tools array and the dispatch function
tool_choice, which must now be set to any
questions.explain: Declare and dispatch. The loop is already generic over the tool set.

questions.q: How does Claude decide which of several tools to call?
options: In the order they appear in the tools array
By schema similarity to the user's phrasing
By whichever tool was used most recently
By reading all the descriptions, every turn
questions.explain: Descriptions, every turn. It is why description quality gets more important as the toolbox grows.

reviewQuestions.q: Can Claude call more than one tool in a single turn?
options: No — only one tool_use block per response
Yes, though it often spreads them over turns
Only when tool_choice has been set to any
Only for the server-side tools it is given
reviewQuestions.explain: It can, and often does not — the conservatism that the batch tool exists to work around.

knowledgePoints.name: Hand it functions, not schemas
knowledgePoints.teach:
The TypeScript, Python and Ruby SDKs ship a tool runner that takes your actual functions, generates the JSON schema from their types and docstrings, and runs the whole exchange internally:

const runner = client.beta.messages.toolRunner({
  model, messages, tools: [getWeather, searchOrders],   // real functions
});
const final = await runner.untilDone();                 // settled final message

What disappears from your code:

  • the while loop,
  • the stop_reason switch,
  • hand-written JSON schemas,
  • manual appending to the message array.

The protocol does not go away. It goes somewhere else.

Which is why the invariants are still worth knowing: when a runner-based agent misbehaves, you are debugging a loop you did not write.

questions.q: What does the SDK tool runner take over?
options: The loop, the switch, schemas, and messages
Tool execution, on Anthropic's own servers
Tool selection, by ranking the descriptions
Authorisation checks on the tool arguments
questions.explain: Four pieces of mechanism. Your functions still run where your code runs, and authorisation is still yours.

questions.q: What does runner.untilDone() return?
options: A stream of every intermediate message
The list of tools that ended up called
The final assistant message, once settled
The last tool_result from the exchange
questions.explain: The settled final message — the loop has already run to end_turn inside it.

reviewQuestions.q: Where do the schemas come from when using the tool runner?
options: You still write them and pass them along
Claude infers them from the function name
Generated from your types and docstrings
They are fetched from a shared registry
reviewQuestions.explain: Generated from your code — which is also a reason to keep docstrings good, since they become the description Claude reads.

knowledgePoints.name: Primitives beat operations
knowledgePoints.teach:
The instinct when an agent fails at a task is to build a tool for that task. Do it a dozen times and you have a dozen narrow tools and an agent that still fails on anything slightly new.

Claude Code's own toolset is the counter-example:

bash   read   write   edit   glob   grep

Not refactor_code. Not install_dependencies. Not run_the_tests. Six primitives that compose, which is how it handles situations nobody designed for: a refactor is grep, then read, then edit, then bash.

Give Claude abstract, combinable tools rather than hyper-specialised ones.

The trade is real. A narrow tool is more reliable at its one job and needs less reasoning to use correctly. What you buy by giving it up is coverage of the long tail — which, for an agent, is most of what it will meet.

questions.q: Your agent has twelve narrow tools and still fails on anything slightly novel. What principle was violated?
options: Tools should be few enough to fit context
Tools should be abstract and combinable
Tools should be server-side where possible
Tools should each do exactly one thing
questions.explain: Specialised tools only cover the cases you predicted. Primitives compose into the ones you did not.

questions.q: Which set illustrates the principle?
options: refactor_code, install_dependencies, run_tests
search_orders, refund_order, cancel_order
bash, read, write, edit, glob, grep
summarise, translate, classify, extract
questions.explain: Claude Code's own toolset — deliberately generic so it can be combined.

options: Reliability on any single predefined job
Nothing — abstract tools are strictly better
The ability to validate the tool inputs
Compatibility with the SDK tool runner
reviewQuestions.explain: A narrow tool is more reliable at its one job. Abstraction trades that for handling what you did not plan for.

knowledgePoints.name: Before acting, look; after acting, look again
knowledgePoints.teach:
Claude can only perceive its environment through tool results.

That sentence is the whole topic. An agent has no eyes. If the loop does not feed it fresh state, it is reasoning about the state it last saw — which may be the state it assumed its last action produced.

Concretely:

BeforeAfter
read a file before editing it, so the edit targets current contentread it back, or check the write's return
list a directory before deciding whether to create a filelist again to confirm it exists
screenshot before clickingscreenshot after, to confirm the click landed

Skipping this is a common source of agent failure. The agent flies blind, repeating or compounding an action that silently failed — and reports success, because from inside the loop nothing contradicted it.

questions.q: An agent reports it saved the file. It did not. Which principle would have caught it?
options: Abstract tools — a narrow save would fail
Forced tool choice, so it cannot be skipped
A lower temperature, for more determinism
Environment inspection — look again after acting
questions.explain: Without an inspection step, nothing in the loop ever contradicts the agent's assumption that the write worked.

questions.q: Why can an agent not simply know whether its action succeeded?
options: Tool results are async and may arrive late
The model does not retain the previous turn
It perceives only through the tool results
Success gets reported only at end_turn
questions.explain: There is no channel other than tool results. Perception is something the loop provides or withholds.

reviewQuestions.q: Why read a file before editing it?
options: To warm the cache before the edit call
So the edit targets the current content
Because edit tools require the contents
To confirm you are authorised to edit
reviewQuestions.explain: The 'before' half of look-act-look. An edit built on remembered content is an edit built on a guess.

knowledgePoints.name: One tool that holds many calls
knowledgePoints.teach:
Claude can call several tools in one turn. It often plays it safe and calls them one at a time, across several turns — and each turn is a full round trip.

The trick is to give it a single tool whose input schema takes an array of sub-invocations:

{
  "name": "batch_tool",
  "description": "Run several independent tool calls at once.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "invocations": {
        "type": "array",
        "items": {"type": "object", "properties": {
          "name":  {"type": "string"},
          "input": {"type": "object"}
        }}
      }
    }
  }
}

Your code unpacks the array, executes each sub-call — optionally in parallel — and returns all the results together as one tool_result.

Use it when the calls are known to be independent. Five city lookups become one round trip instead of five.

The precondition matters: if call two depends on call one's result, batching them is wrong regardless of how much latency it would save.

questions.q: What does batch_tool's input schema accept?
options: A list of tool names to enable this turn
A single tool name plus a repeat count
A nested conversation to run separately
An array of sub-invocations, name and input
questions.explain: An array of {name, input} pairs, which your code unpacks and executes.

questions.q: When is batching the wrong move?
options: When the calls hit the same backend service
When one call's input needs another's result
When there are more than five calls in play
When the tools involved are all server-side
questions.explain: Independence is the precondition. Dependent calls have to be sequential — that is what the sequencing is for.

reviewQuestions.q: What problem does the batch tool solve?
options: Claude calling independent tools one per turn
Claude calling too many at once, hitting limits
Tool results arriving back out of their order
Tool schemas taking up far too much context
reviewQuestions.explain: It collapses N round trips into one by giving the conservative serial habit a single call to express itself through.

knowledgePoints.name: Buffering, and what turning it off costs
knowledgePoints.teach:
By default, when a tool's input JSON streams, the API buffers and validates it — sending only complete top-level key/value pairs at a time.

That produces the delay-then-burst pattern people notice on a large tool input: nothing, nothing, nothing, then a whole field appears at once.

fine_grained = True   # stream chunks as generated; no server-side JSON validation

You gain immediacy. You lose the API's validation safety net.

With it off, your code may observe invalid or partial JSON — Claude might emit a malformed value such as undefined mid-stream — so it must buffer, validate, and recover deliberately rather than parsing each chunk as it lands.

Worth it for a UI that shows arguments filling in live. Not worth it if you were going to wait for the complete input anyway.

questions.q: What causes the delay-then-burst pattern when streaming a large tool input?
options: Network buffering between the SDK and API
Tool inputs are generated after text blocks
Rate limiting applied to streamed tool calls
The API validates and emits complete pairs
questions.explain: Server-side validation holds each pair until it is complete.

questions.q: What must your code handle once fine-grained streaming is on?
options: Content blocks arriving out of their order
Duplicate tool_use ids within one response
Missing stop_reason values on the responses
Partial or invalid JSON, malformed values
questions.explain: You disabled the validation, so its job is now yours: buffer, validate, recover.

reviewQuestions.q: What is the trade-off fine-grained tool streaming makes?
options: Lower cost, set against higher latency
Better tool selection against slower replies
Faster streaming against server-side validation
Larger tool inputs against fewer tools
reviewQuestions.explain: Immediacy for safety. The validation does not disappear — it moves to your code.
